target_customer: Hospitals and neurovascular, cardiac and peripheral interventionalists who perform catheter procedures
problem: Physicians navigate blood vessels with catheters guided only by X-ray images and cannot see inside the vessel in color and real time, which complicates stroke thrombectomy and similar procedures.
business_model: Medical device sales to hospitals (single-use catheters and imaging system)

founders.name: Michael Phillips
education: University of Waterloo, BASc Mechanical Engineering, Entrepreneurship Option (2017)
founders.background_notes: YC page: co-founded during his final undergraduate year; published in the Journal of Neuro-Interventional Surgery and the American Journal of Neuroradiology and holds five granted patents.

founders.name: Phillip Cooper
education: University of Waterloo, BASc Mechanical Engineering, Entrepreneurship Option (2017)
founders.background_notes: Waterloo news article says he co-founded the company with Phillips and was his roommate; the two met in a first-year linear algebra course per The Logic.

technical_complexity.rationale: A camera small enough to fit inside a neurovascular catheter plus medical device regulation, sterile manufacturing and clinical validation; hardware and regulatory heavy for a student-founded team.

defensibility.rationale: Patents (five granted per the YC page), FDA Breakthrough designation and regulatory clearances create barriers that take years to replicate.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Medtronic bought Medina Medical for US$150 million in the neurovascular field, per The Logic; no source shows an incumbent copying the camera, and Vena remains independent.

market_need_then: Stroke thrombectomy and other endovascular procedures relied on indirect X-ray imaging; the company's founders pursued the camera after a university capstone project, and clinical publications and awards (Congress of Neurological Surgeons Innovator of the Year finalist per the YC page) show clinician interest. A dated 2018 demand source was not found.

branding.domain_note: Uses venamed.ca; no acquisition story found.
branding.brand_signature: The world's smallest camera, per the YC page and press
branding.community_and_virality: University of Waterloo and hospital press coverage of the camera; no merch or community evidence.

brand_strength.rationale: Known mainly among clinicians and Waterloo networks through press on the technology; the name is generic and similar to other medical companies.

outcome_analysis: Vena Medical turned a Waterloo capstone project into a miniature intravascular camera, raised about $9M in total by early 2024 mostly from grants and angels, and secured Health Canada approval, FDA Breakthrough designation and FDA clearance for peripheral use in January 2026 with first US commercial cases in April 2026. Progress was slow but steady because of the regulatory path, and the company is still independent.
notes: Competitor search found no dated rival near the 2018 batch (Waterloo, Logic and trade coverage name none), so the list is empty. The roughly $1M angel round is dated 2018 only as the year of YC; The Logic states Y Combinator helped raise it but gives no date or investors. Total about $9M is from The Logic (2024); it also cites about $300,000 in grants and a $50,000 Waterloo prize, not recorded as rounds. Aggregators list only $120K to $290K and conflict. The Series A named on the YC page milestones was not found with amount or date.
